query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under high strain‐rate loading in an inert environment, an initially coarse‐grained single‐phase high‐entropy alloy dynamically evolves an ultra‐nanocrystalline (or partially amorphous) layer along its grain boundaries. This change in microstructure causes localized cavitation or decohesion at the grain boundaries that reduces overall fracture toughness, producing brittle failure modes even in the absence of conventional impurity segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, compositionally complex high‐entropy alloy in its as‐cast state with a coarse-grained microstructure, exhibiting high toughness and ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply high strain‐rate mechanical loading under inert conditions (e.g., in an ultra-high vacuum environment) to minimize temperature rise and suppress thermal diffusion.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at low-to-intermediate temperatures where diffusion is limited, and where the imposed strain rates are sufficiently high to trigger dynamic grain refinement.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline or partially amorphous layer along grain boundaries accompanied by localized nanocavitation.
generation.mechanism: High shear stress from rapid deformation drives grain size reduction below a critical threshold (inverse Hall-Petch regime), shifting the dominant deformation mechanism from dislocation slip to grain-boundary sliding. This dynamic process triggers the formation of a weak, refined boundary layer that is susceptible to cavitation or decohesion, thereby reducing overall toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast coarse-grained baseline, high strain‐rate loaded samples will show reduced ductility and fracture toughness with early onset of grain-boundary cracking characterized by the presence of an amorphous or ultra-fine nanocrystalline boundary region. Conventional signatures of diffusion-driven segregation or intermetallic phase formation should be absent.
generation.baseline: An as-cast, coarse-grained single-phase high-entropy alloy that exhibits high toughness and ductility under low strain-rate conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under service conditions that involve high strain rates and sufficiently low temperatures to minimize thermal diffusion; at higher temperatures or lower strain rates where diffusion becomes active, other mechanisms may prevail.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical strain rate and temperature range required to initiate dynamic boundary amorphization and cavitation remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical single-phase high-entropy alloy specimens. Subject one set to high strain-rate deformation in an inert (ultra-high vacuum) environment to induce dynamic grain refinement, while maintaining a control set under low strain-rate conditions. Use in-situ or post-deformation high-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography to analyze the grain-boundary microstructure, focusing on evidence of ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous layers and cavitation features. Perform standardized fracture toughness tests and compare the fracture modes between the two sets.
measurements: Fracture toughness and ductility from mechanical tensile tests
Grain-boundary structure and grain size distribution using TEM/atom probe tomography
Detection and quantification of nanocavitation sites at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high strain-rate deformed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous grain-boundary layer accompanied by evidence of cavitation, and if their fracture toughness remains similar to that of the low strain-rate (or as-cast) baseline, then the hypothesis that dynamic boundary amorphization leads to brittle behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

drafts.hypothesis: In a high-entropy alloy (HEA) that is initially a single-phase, a service‐relevant exposure (thermal aging possibly combined with moderate mechanical loading) triggers slow, localized grain boundary segregation of one or more slower‐diffusing elements. This in turn leads to nanoscale intergranular precipitate formation that depletes the surrounding matrix of those elements and degrades grain-boundary cohesion, eventually causing a transition from ductile to brittle behavior.
drafts.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex HEA with a homogeneous, single‐phase microstructure and high toughness.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy to controlled thermal aging at an intermediate service temperature (with and without moderate mechanical loading) that is sufficient to activate grain boundary diffusion without inducing complete phase transformation.
drafts.conditions: Service-like conditions where diffusion is activated (e.g., intermediate temperatures and relevant holding times) and mechanical stresses that simulate demanding engineering loads; comparisons should also be made against similarly processed conventional alloys.
drafts.structural_mediator: Grain boundary segregation followed by nanoscale intergranular precipitate formation.
drafts.mechanism: Slow diffusion under service conditions leads to selective segregation of one or more elements at the grain boundaries. The localized accumulation promotes the nucleation of nanoscale precipitates which both deplete the adjacent matrix and reduce the cohesion of the grain boundaries, setting the stage for brittle crack initiation under stress.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Thermally aged (and/or mechanically loaded) HEA samples will exhibit measurable increases in grain boundary segregation and formation of nanoscale precipitates, accompanied by a reduction in fracture toughness relative to the as-cast baseline. In a controlled comparison, conventional alloys are expected to show more rapid or extensive intermetallic formation by different mechanisms, thereby distinguishing the HEA’s unique pathway to embrittlement.
drafts.baseline: The alloy in its as-cast, single-phase state with a homogeneous elemental distribution, high fracture toughness, and no detectable grain boundary segregation or precipitates.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be active under intermediate service conditions where diffusion is activated but temperatures are not so high as to cause widespread phase changes; it may not apply at very low temperatures (insufficient diffusion) or extremely high temperatures (where complete phase transformation or grain growth might dominate).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of identical, as-cast HEA specimens. Subject one group to intermediate thermal aging (with and without applying moderate mechanical loading) while keeping a control group at ambient conditions. Employ advanced characterization techniques (e.g., TEM, atom-probe tomography, and EDS) to examine grain boundary composition and detect nanoscale precipitates. Conduct fracture toughness tests to quantify any degradation. Include a comparison with conventional alloys processed under the same conditions to highlight differences in embrittlement behavior.
measurements: Comparative mechanical response tests on conventional alloy samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged (and/or mechanically loaded) HEA samples do not exhibit significant grain boundary segregation and/or formation of nanoscale precipitates, or if there is no measurable reduction in fracture toughness relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis that service-induced grain boundary segregation and precipitate formation drive the brittle transition in HEAs is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Under service-like thermal or mechanical loading, initially single‐phase high‐entropy alloys develop nanoscale compositional segregation at grain boundaries that induces local ordering and reduces interfacial cohesion, thereby triggering brittle failure. This mechanism differs from the classical grain‐boundary precipitation seen in conventional alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase compositionally complex high‐entropy alloy with uniformly distributed elements and fine grains.
drafts.intervention: Expose specimens to prolonged service-mimicking conditions (e.g., high-temperature aging or cyclic low-temperature impact loading) while conducting detailed microstructural analyses.
drafts.conditions: Use identical processing and loading conditions for the HEA and, as a controlled comparison, for a conventional alloy known to degrade toughness through grain-boundary precipitation. Ensure that the thermal exposures or mechanical loading durations are sufficient to induce diffusion-controlled segregation without triggering gross phase separation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoscale compositional segregation and subtle ordering at the grain boundaries, which may manifest as small clusters or ordered regions not forming distinct intermetallic precipitates.
drafts.mechanism: Service conditions enhance the mobility of constituent elements in a high-entropy matrix, driving them to segregate at grain boundaries. This local enrichment promotes short-range ordering that depletes the grain boundary strength, making them preferential sites for crack initiation and propagation, distinct from the coarse, brittle precipitates typically observed in conventional alloys.
drafts.predicted_outcome: In HEAs subjected to these conditions, toughness degradation will correlate with an increase in nanoscale segregation and local ordering at the grain boundaries observed via atom-probe tomography or high-resolution TEM, even though no obvious macroscopic intermetallic phases develop. The conventional alloy, in contrast, would show visible grain-boundary precipitates under similar conditions.
drafts.baseline: The initial microstructure, characterized by uniform elemental distribution and high fracture toughness in the as-processed state.
drafts.boundary: This behavior is expected under extended service conditions that promote atomic diffusion without reaching temperatures or stresses that cause full-scale phase transformations or grain coarsening. The hypothesis is bounded by conditions where diffusion is active but gross compositional partitioning is not yet dominant.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA specimens. Subject one set to prolonged service-simulating conditions (thermal aging or cyclic mechanical loading) and keep the other as an unaged control. Conduct identical tests on a conventional alloy sample expected to form visible grain-boundary precipitates. Use high-resolution techniques such as atom-probe tomography and transmission electron microscopy to assess grain-boundary compositional profiles and ordering. Perform fracture toughness tests on all specimens.
measurements: Grain boundary elemental segregation profiles (via atom-probe tomography)
Local ordering or cluster formation (via high-resolution TEM/diffraction)
Fracture toughness or crack propagation metrics (mechanical testing)
Comparison of microstructural features in HEA vs. conventional alloy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA samples do not exhibit an increase in nanoscale segregation or local ordering at the grain boundaries following service conditions—or if measured toughness degradation in the HEA cannot be correlated with these subtle structural changes (i.e., if brittleness only appears in association with visible intermetallic precipitates similar to conventional alloys)—then the mechanism as hypothesized is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In a single‐phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (HEA), brittle behavior can emerge not from static impurity segregation or the precipitation of intermetallics, as in conventional alloys, but from a dynamically induced transition. Under service-relevant loading (e.g., high strain rate or intermediate temperatures) the alloy undergoes extreme grain refinement that results in an ultra-nanocrystalline surface or near-boundary layer. This transition suppresses conventional intragranular dislocation activity and favors grain boundary sliding. The markedly refined (and possibly amorphous) grain boundary regions then promote localized cavitation and decohesion, leading to a reduction in toughness and an apparent brittle failure even without the classical signs of segregation or secondary phase formation.
drafts.material_initial_state: An initially coarse-grained, single-phase, compositionally complex HEA (for example, a typical FCC HEA like CoCrFeMnNi) with a solid solution structure and no significant grain-boundary segregation.
drafts.intervention: Subject the HEA to controlled high strain-rate deformation (such as sliding contact or high-rate mechanical testing) in an inert environment (e.g., ultra-high vacuum or chemically inert atmosphere) so that temperature increases are minimal and impurity-driven segregation is avoided.
drafts.conditions: Intermediate service temperatures and high strain rates where dynamic grain refinement is expected, but below levels that would induce conventional diffusion-driven precipitation or impurity segregation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Transformation of the microstructure via dynamic refinement into an ultra-nanocrystalline layer at or near grain boundaries which then develop cavitation (nanoporosity) due to reduced cohesive strength.
drafts.mechanism: Under high strain rate loading, severe plastic deformation drives rapid grain refinement. Once the grain size drops below a critical threshold (inverse Hall-Petch regime), the material’s ability to undergo dislocation-mediated plasticity is diminished. Instead, grain boundary sliding becomes dominant, and the low effective cohesion at the ultra-nanocrystalline boundaries leads to cavitation and decohesion. This dynamic amorphization of the grain boundaries weakens overall toughness, resulting in brittle-like behavior.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial coarse-grained baseline, the HEA will exhibit reduced ductility and fracture toughness after high strain-rate deformation, with microstructural evidence (via TEM/atom probe) of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer and cavitation (nanoporosity) localized along grain boundaries. In contrast, conventional alloys would only show brittleness when static impurity segregation or intermetallic precipitation occurs.
drafts.baseline: Initial mechanical properties (toughness and ductility) of the coarse-grained single-phase HEA measured before applying high strain-rate deformation under inert conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies under service conditions (i.e., intermediate temperatures and high strain rates) where diffusion is limited and impurity segregation is minimal; at higher temperatures where diffusion becomes significant classical segregation and precipitation mechanisms may additionally affect toughness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same coarse-grained single-phase HEA specimens. Deform one set under high strain-rate conditions in an inert (ultra-high vacuum) environment and a control set under low strain rate. Use high-resolution TEM/atom probe tomography post-deformation to measure grain size distributions and identify grain boundary cavitation (nanoporosity). Concurrently, perform mechanical testing to assess changes in toughness and ductility.
measurements: Presence and size of cavitation-induced nanopores (atom probe tomography)
Fracture toughness and ductility (mechanical tensile testing)
Shear strength or friction coefficient (tribological measurement, if applicable)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high strain-rate deformation does not result in a statistically significant reduction in toughness and ductility accompanied by the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer with evidence of cavitation (compared to the control), then the dynamic amorphization and cavitation mechanism would be falsified as the primary cause for brittle behavior in the HEA.

drafts.hypothesis: Under high strain-rate deformation in a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, the intense shear induces dynamic amorphization along grain boundaries, which in turn weakens the intergranular cohesion (via cavitation or decohesion) and produces a brittle behavior that is not driven by conventional impurity segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
drafts.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, coarse-grained compositionally complex HEA (e.g. equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) exhibiting high toughness and ductility.
drafts.intervention: Apply high strain-rate loading (such as sliding contact or uniaxial tension) under controlled inert (UHV or oxygen-free) conditions so that temperature rise is minimal and grain-boundary segregation is suppressed.
drafts.conditions: Tests performed at low to moderate temperatures in inert or ultra-high vacuum environments, where traditional thermal segregation is negligible, and the strain rate is sufficiently high to induce extreme grain refinement near grain boundaries.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous grain-boundary layer generated dynamically by severe plastic deformation.
drafts.mechanism: High shear stresses refine grains below a critical size (inverse Hall-Petch regime), suppressing dislocation-mediated plasticity in favor of grain-boundary sliding. This rapid refinement leads to dynamic amorphization and cavitation along grain boundaries, which weakens intergranular cohesion and triggers brittle fracture even in the absence of classical segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to an undeformed, coarse-grained baseline, the high strain-rate loaded alloy will display reduced toughness marked by early, localized crack initiation along grain boundaries that show amorphous or ultra-fine nanocrystalline structure, rather than evidence of impurity-driven precipitates.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast, single-phase HEA with coarse grains exhibits high ductility and toughness under low strain-rate conditions without intergranular amorphous layers.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under service conditions where loading rates are high and temperatures are low enough to avoid thermally activated grain-boundary segregation. Under slower loading or higher temperature conditions where thermal effects dominate, the mechanism is less likely to be the controlling factor.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the HEA: one set remains in the as-cast, coarse-grained state while the other is subjected to high strain-rate deformation in an ultra-high vacuum environment to induce dynamic amorphization. Conduct standardized tensile tests on both sets while performing in-situ microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM or STEM) focusing on the grain boundaries.
measurements: Tensile fracture toughness and ductility (stress-strain behavior)
In-situ electron microscopy imaging of grain-boundary structure (to detect amorphous/ultra-nanocrystalline layers)
Grain size distribution analysis in deformed regions
Local mechanical property measurements (e.g., nanoindentation) at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high strain-rate deformed samples do not exhibit grain-boundary amorphization or associated localized decohesion (i.e. if their toughness remains comparable to that of the baseline coarse-grained state and fracture occurs via conventional mechanisms), then the hypothesis of dynamic amorphization causing brittle behavior is falsified.
